# Part A — Multiple Choice

### Question 1 — ETC location {#w10-mc01}
The electron-transport chain is embedded primarily in the:

- **A.** outer mitochondrial membrane
- **B.** plasma membrane of animal cells
- **C.** inner mitochondrial membrane
- **D.** nuclear envelope

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
:::

### Question 2 — Matrix {#w10-mc02}
Which process takes place in the mitochondrial matrix?

- **A.** proton accumulation during ETC activity
- **B.** glycogen storage only
- **C.** extracellular signaling
- **D.** pyruvate oxidation and the CAC

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
:::

### Question 3 — Cristae {#w10-mc03}
Cristae primarily increase:

- **A.** nuclear volume
- **B.** inner-membrane surface area for respiratory proteins
- **C.** DNA replication rate
- **D.** glucose concentration in cytosol

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}

### Question 7 — Why FAD matters {#w10-mc07}
The ability of FAD/FADH2 to handle one or two electrons is useful because:

- **A.** it can bridge carriers that move electron pairs and carriers that move single electrons

- **D.** it directly phosphorylates ADP

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}

### Question 31 {#w10-mc31}

Which answer addresses BOTH ATP-synthesis substrates and their access to the matrix?

- **A.** NADH and CO2 freely diffuse to ATP synthase as its chemical substrates.
- **B.** Pi is made from oxygen and requires no transport.
- **C.** ADP and Pi are supplied by inner-membrane transport proteins.
- **D.** Only ADP is required, and the membrane has no effect on entry.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.** ADP and Pi are supplied by inner-membrane transport proteins.

Lecture 10:20 names ADP and Pi and explicitly states that they enter through transport proteins. Naming ATP synthase alone does not answer the transport part.

**Related objectives:** W10-07
:::

### Question 32 {#w10-mc32}

Which description separates the rotary and stationary components of ATP synthase?

- **A.** The rotor/γ shaft turns while the αβ dimers change conformation without rotating as a rigid head.
- **B.** All αβ dimers rotate together while γ remains immobile.
- **C.** The rotor is a freely soluble enzyme in the cytosol.
- **D.** No component moves or changes conformation during ATP synthesis.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.** The rotor/γ shaft turns while the αβ dimers change conformation without rotating as a rigid head.

The lecture's rotational-catalysis explanation links proton movement to shaft rotation and conformational changes in the stationary catalytic head.

**Related objectives:** W10-08
:::

### Question 33 {#w10-mc33}

Which label set correctly describes the four mitochondrial regions?

- **A.** Outer membrane; intermembrane space; cristae-bearing inner membrane; matrix inside the inner membrane.
- **B.** Outer membrane; nucleus; cytosol; cristae outside the cell.
- **C.** Matrix; endoplasmic reticulum; Golgi apparatus; intercellular space.
- **D.** One membrane surrounding an undivided matrix with no intermembrane space.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.** Outer membrane; intermembrane space; cristae-bearing inner membrane; matrix inside the inner membrane.

The relative positions matter for proton pumping: matrix to intermembrane space across the inner membrane.

**Related objectives:** W10-01
:::

### Question 34 {#w10-mc34}

Why is “FADH2 carries one electron” an incomplete interpretation of the lecture?

- **A.** FADH2 must always donate four electrons simultaneously.
- **B.** Only cytochromes can ever be reduced.
- **C.** FADH2 carries no electrons and only transports ATP.
- **D.** Fully reduced FADH2 holds two electrons; the carrier can transfer one or two at a time.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.** Fully reduced FADH2 holds two electrons; the carrier can transfer one or two at a time.

The distinction is between electron content of the reduced carrier and the possible size of an individual transfer step.

**Related objectives:** W10-02,W10-03
:::

### Question 35 {#w10-mc35}

With thermogenin active, what is the expected energy partition relative to fully coupled respiration?

- **A.** Less ATP captured per fuel oxidized and more heat as protons bypass ATP synthase.
- **B.** No fuel oxidation can occur under any condition.
- **C.** No heat because the proton gradient is never dissipated.
- **D.** More ATP because every proton must pass through ATP synthase.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.** Less ATP captured per fuel oxidized and more heat as protons bypass ATP synthase.

UCP1 provides a route for proton return without ATP-synthase capture; it does not mean that all electron transport must stop.

**Related objectives:** W10-09,W11-01
:::

# Part B — Every Learning Objective

Answer each prompt before opening its model answer. The source sheet supplies the objective; the task underneath makes the required components explicit.

### Objective W10-01 — Mitochondrial structure {#w10-lo01}

**Original objective:** Be clear on mitochondrial structure

Name the four regions, place the ETC, ATP synthase, proton accumulation and PDH/CAC, and explain why cristae matter.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The outer membrane surrounds the organelle. The intermembrane space is between the membranes and is the side to which respiratory complexes pump H+. The inner membrane is highly selective, forms cristae and contains the ETC and ATP synthase. The matrix lies inside the inner membrane and contains the PDH/CAC machinery. Cristae provide membrane area for respiratory proteins; the lecture links denser cristae with high respiratory activity. See the coverage page's source note about the conflicting wording on slide 10:3.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 1; Lecture 10:4–10:6; Alberts Ch. 14.
:::

### Objective W10-02 — One- and two-electron carriers {#w10-lo02}

**Original objective:** Be clear on how many electrons NADH and FADH2 carry and understand the importance of FADH2 being able to donate and accept either 1 or 2 electrons at a time

Explain the electron capacity of NADH and FADH2 AND why the one-/two-electron distinction matters.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
NADH carries two electrons and transfers a pair. Fully reduced FADH2 also holds two electrons, but the flavin carrier can undergo one- or two-electron transfer steps. That flexibility bridges two-electron donors and one-electron carriers such as cytochromes. “One or two at a time” describes transfer flexibility, not that fully reduced FADH2 contains only one electron.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 2; Lecture 10:7; Tutorial 6.
:::

### Objective W10-03 — Cytochromes {#w10-lo03}

**Original objective:** Be clear that cytochromes carry 1 electron at a time

How many electrons does a cytochrome transfer per step, and what part changes oxidation state?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cytochromes transfer **one electron at a time**. Their heme iron cycles between Fe3+ and Fe2+ as it accepts or donates an electron. Do not assign the two-electron transfer behavior of NADH to a single cytochrome step.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 3; Lecture 10:8.
:::

### Objective W10-04 — Conserving electron-transfer energy {#w10-lo04}

**Original objective:** Be clear that the potential energy conserved as electrons are moving down the electron transport chain is used to pump protons

Explain what electron-transfer energy is used for directly, and distinguish that from ATP formation.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Stepwise electron transfer toward oxygen releases free energy. Respiratory complexes conserve part of it by pumping H+ out of the matrix, establishing an electrochemical gradient. They do not directly transfer a phosphate to ADP. ATP synthase later uses proton return to drive ATP synthesis.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 4; Lecture 10:9–10:16.
:::

### Objective W10-05 — Proton-motive force {#w10-lo05}

**Original objective:** What is the proton motive force

Define the proton-motive force and state BOTH components.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It is the electrochemical driving force across the inner mitochondrial membrane. One component is the H+ concentration difference (chemical or pH gradient); the other is the electrical potential from charge separation. Both favor proton return toward the matrix in the respiring mitochondrion shown in the lecture.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 5; Lecture 10:14.
:::

### Objective W10-06 — Proton pumps and direction {#w10-lo06}

**Original objective:** Which components of the Electron Transport Chain pump protons and what is the directionality

Identify the proton-pumping complexes, the non-pumping complex, and the directions of pumping and ATP-synthase proton return.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Complexes **I, III and IV** pump H+ **from matrix to intermembrane space**. Complex II transfers electrons but does not pump protons. During ATP synthesis, H+ returns **from intermembrane space to matrix through ATP synthase**. Distinguish electron flow along the chain from proton movement across the membrane.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 6; Lecture 10:14–10:18.
:::

### Objective W10-07 — ATP substrates and matrix entry {#w10-lo07}

**Original objective:** What are the substrate for ATP synthesis and how do they get into the matrix

Name BOTH substrates and explain how they reach the matrix; do not stop at naming ATP synthase.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The substrates are **ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi)**. They reach the matrix through inner-membrane transport proteins, rather than freely diffusing through the membrane. Adenine-nucleotide transport exchanges ADP into the matrix for ATP leaving it; phosphate is transported in by a phosphate transport system. ATP synthase then uses matrix-side ADP and Pi. The lecture's required general answer is “through transport proteins”; carrier names are supporting detail, not an extra memorization requirement.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 7; Lecture 10:20; Alberts Ch. 14.
:::

### Objective W10-08 — ATP synthase conformations {#w10-lo08}

**Original objective:** What happens in each of the three conformations of the alpha-beta dimers of ATP synthase

State the role of Loose, Tight and Open and explain how proton movement changes the stationary dimers.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Loose:** ADP and Pi enter and are held. **Tight:** ATP is formed. **Open:** ATP is released. Proton flow through the membrane Fo region drives the rotor and central γ shaft. The three αβ dimers remain stationary but change conformation as γ turns, so each catalytic site progresses through the states. Do not say the αβ head rotates as one rigid wheel.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 8; Lecture 10:21–10:24; Tutorial 6.
:::

### Objective W10-09 — Thermogenin {#w10-lo09}

**Original objective:** What is thermogenin

Identify thermogenin, its location and its effects on proton return, ATP yield and heat.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Thermogenin (UCP1) is an uncoupling protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown-adipose mitochondria. It permits proton return toward the matrix without driving ATP synthase. Consequently less gradient energy is captured in ATP and more is dissipated as heat. Fuel oxidation and electron transport can continue; thermogenin is not simply an ETC inhibitor.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 9; Lecture 10, thermogenin slides; Tutorial 6.
:::

# Part C — Integrated Practice

### Integrated Question 1 — Oxygen removal
Predict what happens to electron flow, proton pumping, and ATP synthesis if oxygen is suddenly removed.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Without oxygen as the final electron acceptor, electron flow through the ETC backs up, proton pumping declines, the proton-motive force collapses, and oxidative ATP synthesis falls sharply.
:::

### Integrated Question 2 — Complex II mutation
A mutation prevents Complex II from transferring electrons but leaves I, III, and IV normal. Which electron source is most directly impaired?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Electron entry associated with **FADH2/succinate oxidation** is most directly impaired because Complex II is the entry point for those electrons.
:::

### Integrated Question 3 — Inner membrane leak
Why would a proton-leaky inner membrane decrease ATP production even if NADH oxidation continues?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The leak dissipates the proton-motive force. Electron transport can still release energy and pump protons, but the stored gradient cannot build sufficiently to power ATP synthase efficiently.
:::

### Integrated Question 4 — Brown fat
Explain why brown adipose tissue can consume fuel and oxygen while generating relatively less ATP and more heat.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Thermogenin allows protons to bypass ATP synthase. Electron transport and proton pumping continue, but gradient energy is dissipated as heat instead of being efficiently captured in ATP.
:::

### Integrated Question 5 — ETC versus ATP synthase
In one sentence, distinguish the jobs of the ETC and ATP synthase.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The ETC uses electron-transfer energy to build a proton gradient, whereas ATP synthase uses the energy stored in that gradient to make ATP from ADP and Pi.
:::
